cards.explanation: The answer is honor. The verse says, "Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, honor does not befit a fool." Snow in summer and rain at harvest both show up where they don't belong, and so does honor on a fool. If I opened my bakery door in July and found a snowman waiting in line, I'd have questions.

The answer is False, friends. The verse says, "Like a fluttering sparrow or darting swallow, an undeserved curse does not come to rest." Try getting a swallow to sit still on your counter. It's not happening, and neither is the curse landing. I know because I watched birds from a kitchen window, not a drawer.

The reason is that you'll end up like him. The verse says, "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him." Match his folly and now there are two of you doing it. Two people arguing nonsense in a kitchen is just a louder kitchen.

The reason Solomon gives is so he won't be wise in his own eyes. The verse says, "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes." It sits right after the line that says don't answer him that way. Two lines, side by side, and the text doesn't stop to explain how they fit together. I'm just gonna stand here with my mustache scratching my chin.

The answer is True. The verse says, "Like cutting off one’s own feet or drinking violence is the sending of a message by the hand of a fool." Sending a message by a fool is put right next to cutting off your own feet. Friends, that's a rough review for a delivery service.

The word is proverb. The verse says, "Like lame legs hanging limp is a proverb in the mouth of a fool." Legs hanging limp can't carry anybody anywhere. A wise saying in a fool's mouth is like that, with no strength behind it.

The one compared to the archer is the one who hires a fool or passerby. The verse says, "Like an archer who wounds at random is he who hires a fool or passerby." The one doing the hiring is the one in the picture. Wild shots, friends.

The word is repeats. The verse says, "As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly." It's a rough picture, friends. He goes back to the same folly again. I once reached for the same hot pan twice in one morning, so I'm not judging.

The answer is False. The verse says, "Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him." Somebody who thinks he's already got it all figured out is hard to teach. I'd rather be a fool with an open mind and a warm oven.

The slacker announces that a lion is in the road. He says, "A lion is in the road! A fierce lion roams the public square!" It's a big, scary announcement, and it happens to be a great reason to stay inside. I think we've all had a reason like that on a Monday morning.

The word is bed. The verse says, "As a door turns on its hinges, so the slacker turns on his bed." A door swings back and forth and stays right where it's attached. The slacker rolls over and goes nowhere either.

The answer is False. The verse says, "The slacker buries his hand in the dish; it wearies him to bring it back to his mouth." His hand is in the dish, but lifting it is the hard part. Nobody's empty-dish champion here.

The slacker thinks he's wiser than seven men who answer discreetly. The verse says, "The slacker is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer discreetly." He's measuring himself against seven careful men and coming out ahead. That's a whole lot of confidence for a slacker.

The answer is a dog. The verse says, "Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own." Grabbing a dog by the ears is a quick way to get yourself in the middle of something. Same goes for walking into an argument that isn't yours.

The answer is True. The verse says, "Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows, so is the man who deceives his neighbor…" Then he says he was only joking. Calling it a joke afterward doesn't un-shoot the arrows. A joke that burns somebody isn't a joke.

Wood goes in the first blank and gossip goes in the second. The verse says, "Without wood, a fire goes out; without gossip, a conflict ceases." No wood, no fire, and my ovens agree with that one. A fight needs something to feed on, and gossip is that something. Take it away and the conflict stops.

The words go down into the inmost being. The verse says, "The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being." The picture is food going down. The place it lands is the inmost being.

The answer is False. The verse says, "Like glaze covering an earthen vessel are burning lips and a wicked heart." It's not a wise man's kind words. It's burning lips and a wicked heart, shiny on the outside like glaze on a clay pot.

Solomon says do not believe him. The verse says, "When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart." Gracious words on the outside, seven abominations on the inside. That's a cookie box with a pretty ribbon and nothing good in it.

The answer is False. The verse says, "Though his hatred is concealed by deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly." His hatred is concealed for now. The verse says his wickedness will be exposed.
The one who digs a pit falls into it. The verse says, "He who digs a pit will fall into it…" The one who digs the pit is the one who falls into it. Dig carefully, friends.

The answer is True. The last verse says, "A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth causes ruin." The flattering mouth sits right beside the lying tongue. Sweet talk can still leave a mess, friends.
